facts.claim: Screen time is linked to poorer sleep outcomes in infants, toddlers and preschoolers.
facts.quote: Results indicate that screen time is associated with poorer sleep outcomes in infants, toddlers and preschoolers.

facts.claim: Excessive screen time is linked to shorter sleep duration among toddlers and preschoolers.
facts.quote: Strong evidence of the meta-analysis suggested that excessive screen time was associated with overweight/obesity and shorter sleep duration among toddlers and preschoolers.

facts.claim: Excessive screen time is linked to disrupted sleep.
facts.quote: Excessive screen time ([Formula: see text] 2 h per day) is associated with childhood overweight and obesity, physical inactivity, increased sedentary time, unfavorable dietary behaviors, and disrupted sleep.

facts.claim: Sleep latency, percentages of stage 1 and stage 2 significantly increased with age in adults.
facts.quote: In adults, it appeared that sleep latency, percentages of stage 1 and stage 2 significantly increased with age while percentage of REM sleep decreased.

research.angle: While screen time is linked to poorer sleep outcomes and shorter sleep duration in infants, toddlers, and preschoolers, meta-analysis did not confirm these unfavorable associations in preschoolers.
research.verdict: The evidence shows a link between screen time and poorer sleep in young children, but the strength and consistency of this association vary by age group.
research.caveat: The overall quality of evidence for these associations in children under 5 was reported as very low.
